analysis.one_liner: Sets a federal test making it easier to classify gig and service workers as independent contractors rather than employees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on February 2, 2023 and never advanced; it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a narrow definition of "employee" into federal wage law. Under its test, a worker counts as an independent contractor — not an employee — if they control the key parts of their work and can make a profit or take a loss based on their own initiative. Independent contractors fall outside the Fair Labor Standards Act's minimum wage, overtime pay, and other workplace protections. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig and app-based platform companies — ride-hailing, delivery, and freelance marketplaces — are the main beneficiaries. A statutory contractor-friendly test would lower their labor costs by keeping workers out of minimum wage and overtime rules and off company payroll for benefits and payroll taxes. Some workers who genuinely run their own businesses would also benefit from clearer rules and preserved flexibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig platforms and companies using contract labor

how_it_helps.text: It writes a statutory test into the Fair Labor Standards Act under which a worker is 'likely' an independent contractor if they control key aspects of the work and can profit or lose money based on their own initiative and investments [S2][S3].

It directs the Department of Labor to look only at what actually happens between the worker and the company, ignoring contractual labels or expectations that are not regularly met in practice — a provision aimed at preventing companies from winning contractor status with paperwork alone [S3].

It allows the Department of Labor to weigh secondary factors, such as whether the work requires specialized skills and whether it is performed continuously as part of an integrated unit, when the main test is not decisive [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers classified as independent contractors under the new test would bear the cost: they would lose access to the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and the employer-side payroll contributions that fund Social Security and unemployment insurance. Workers who want employee status and the protections that come with it would have a harder time getting reclassified.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers kept out of employee protections

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove workers from the FLSA's minimum wage and overtime protections. Under the two-part test, a worker who 'exercises substantial control over key aspects' of the work and can 'earn profits or incur losses' is likely an independent contractor — a description that fits many gig app workers who in practice depend on a single platform for their income [S2][S3].

The test lets the Department of Labor treat a worker as an independent contractor even when the work is continuous, year-round, and performed as part of the company's operation, as long as it requires some specialized skill — so long-term, full-time-style workers could still be kept out of employee status [S2].

Critics of contractor-friendly tests argue they shift costs onto workers: no overtime, no employer share of payroll taxes, no unemployment insurance contributions, and no expense reimbursement. The bill's sponsors frame the same rules as protecting flexibility and entrepreneurship, but the bill text does not provide any substitute benefits or minimum earnings floor for workers classified as contractors [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's cost is the central issue. Reclassifying millions of app-based and service workers as independent contractors would keep them outside the wage floor, overtime pay, and workplace protections that the Fair Labor Standards Act provides to employees [S2][S3]. That is a real gain in flexibility for the few who genuinely run their own businesses, but it is a pay cut and a protection loss for workers whose platforms actually control their work. The bill does include one modest safeguard — it ignores paper contracts that the parties do not follow in practice, so companies cannot escape employee status with a label alone [S3] — but that does not offset the loss of baseline protections. The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, so none of these effects took place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ferguson introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with seven original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
No further action appears in the record after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action are listed in the bill's action history [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing, so the measure died with the Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig and app-based platform companies benefit, because the contractor-friendly classification test they favored never became law — but neither did anything else, so the existing classification rules and pending regulatory fights over worker status simply carried on unchanged. Gig workers who would have lost minimum wage and overtime protections are better off that the bill failed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gig platforms; status quo rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. A. Drew Ferguson IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 2, 2023 and led its advocacy [S1][S3].

for.name: 11 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 11 cosponsors were Republicans, including original cosponsors Mrs. Miller of West Virginia, Mr. Garcia, Mr. Austin Scott, Mrs. Hageman, Mr. Cole, and Mr. McClintock [S3][S4].

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat with the committee from February 2023 until the Congress ended with no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never moved past a party-line-supported referral [S4].

industries.industry: Gig and app-based platform companies (ride-hailing, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: A statutory contractor-friendly test would lower labor costs by keeping workers outside minimum wage, overtime, and payroll-tax rules. Companies and workers who prefer flexibility both gain; workers who depend on a single platform for steady income lose baseline protections.

industries.industry: Gig and freelance workers who rely on platform work for full-time income
industries.note: Workers classified as independent contractors lose minimum wage, overtime, employer payroll-tax contributions, and expense reimbursement under the FLSA. Some genuinely independent professionals keep flexibility they already had; the change mainly hurts workers whose 'control' is nominal.

industries.industry: Traditional employers that use contract labor (staffing, construction subcontracting, delivery)
industries.note: A clearer, narrower definition of 'employee' reduces the risk that misclassified contract workers are reclassified as employees owed back wages and overtime. The bill also lets the Labor Department ignore contractual labels not met in practice, limiting how far a company can stretch the category, but the overall effect favors the contracting model.
